title: IM952 - Big Data Research: Hype or Revolution?
text:
This repository contains the lab materials for IM952: Big Data Research: Hype or Revolution?, taught at the Centre for Interdisciplinary Methodologies at the University of Warwick.
In the next three lab sessions, we will be replicating an ongoing research project that uses a data-centric approach to interrogate about considerations of data production and EDI. There are three main learning outcomes:

title: IM952 Labs
text:
The problem

Historically, Maps and power have gone hand in hand.(Crampton 2009; Harley 2008; Wood 1992)

Maps are never neutral: they have a political agenda (Haraway 1988; Harley 1989; Monmonier 2018)
Historically used for domination, control and/or surveillance (Foucault 1995; Scott 2020; Graham 2005; Edney 1999)




Critical and Feminist Geography have critiqued map’s objectivity:

Flagging (unconscious) bias by map-makers (usually men) (Monk and Hanson 1982)
Challenging positivist approaches and based exclusively in quantification (Pickles 1995)
Highlighting importance on what is being presented and silenced (Pavlovskaya 2009; Kwan 2002; d’Ignazio and Klein 2020)

title: IM952 Labs
text:
Object of study

OpenStreetMap: more than a map

OSM is the biggest and most precise free/libre spatial database of the world

It’s a Geospatial Database

9.1 billion nodes (2024-03-31) | Data under Open Database License (ODbL)
Flexible data structure based on key = value pairs

It is also a map (or a series of maps)

that have an opinionated representation of the database

It is a global and huge community (of 10,000,000 users worldwide!):

Anyone can contribute to it:
Adding / Editing map
Deciding what is included and how is represented

Session’s goals

Familiarise with the dataset (and the process it represents)
learn tidyverse’s syntax for frequent data manipulations:

filter() to subset rows matching some conditions
select(), to subset columns (by name or position)
group() and summarise() to compute summaries based on some criteria
join_by() to combine datasets

learn when to apply these methods to address research questions

Tagging proposals


Anyone can suggest what to tag and/or how to tag it. Process documented here.

Create a wiki page describing the proposal and its rationale
Request for Comments
Address every comment
Voting

Min 8 votes
Min 3 positive votes per 1 negative vote






Source: https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Proposal:Lgbtq

title: Data
text:
The data
The data consists of two `csv` files:

proposals.csv: containing all Approved, Rejected and Proposed tagging proposals from the OSM Wiki, as well as their associated metadata.
proposals_votes.csv: containing all the votes cast for every tagging proposal in proposals.

Both files were generated using a dedicated R-package called {OSMproposals} (Cámara-Menoyo 2026) which provides reproducible datasets containing information about OpenStreetMap’s tagging proposals. It does so by querying and webscrapping OSM’s wiki via helper functions. Refer to the official documentation page: https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/ to see metadata and the source code that generated each dataset.






WarningImportant considerations




The provided datasets contain experimental versions of the actual datasets provided by the package, so documentation may slightly differ.
These datasets are part of an ongoing research. Please, do not share them beyond the classroom unless with explicit permission from their authors.




Loading data
The data is provided by you in the data/ folder. We’ll load the two datasets and assign them, respectively, to the variables proposals and proposals_votes:

# Load dependencies
library(dplyr)

path_proposals <- "data/raw/proposals.csv"
path_votes <- "data/raw/proposals_votes.csv"

proposals <- read.csv(path_proposals) 
proposals_votes <- read.csv(path_votes)



Exploring data
Some questions we may want to immediately answer to familiarise with the datasets are:

How big are these datasets?
What do they contain?

1. Interrogating data locally
text: In this week, you will be using your laptops to work with a relatively big research dataset to answer actual research questions that arose from a research project.

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
Session’s goals

Familiarise with the dataset (and the process it represents)
learn tidyverse’s syntax for frequent data manipulations:

filter() to subset rows matching some conditions
select(), to subset columns (by name or position)
group() and summarise() to compute summaries based on some criteria
join_by() to combine datasets

learn when to apply these methods to address research questions

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
Slides

Open the slides in full screen

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
The data
The data consists of two csv files:

proposals.csv: containing all Approved, Rejected and Proposed tagging proposals from the OSM Wiki, as well as their associated metadata.
proposals_votes.csv: containing all the votes cast for every tagging proposal in proposals.

Both files were generated using a dedicated R-package called {OSMproposals} (Cámara-Menoyo 2026) which provides reproducible datasets containing information about OpenStreetMap’s tagging proposals. It does so by querying and webscrapping OSM’s wiki via helper functions. Refer to the official documentation page: https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/ to see metadata and the source code that generated each dataset.

Cámara-Menoyo, Carlos. 2026. OSMpRoposals: Reproducible Datasets about OpenStreetMap’s Tagging Proposals. https://warwickcim.github.io/osmproposals/.






WarningImportant considerations




The provided datasets contain experimental versions of the actual datasets provided by the package, so documentation may slightly differ.
These datasets are part of an ongoing research. Please, do not share them beyond the classroom unless with explicit permission from their authors.









CautionIs this big data?





There are two ways in which data can be considered as big data:(Matter 2024):

Data that is difficult to handle: this could be either often because it has been “gathered from unorthodox sources, providing poorly structured data (e.g., raw text, web pages, images, etc.) as well as because of the infrastructure needed to store and load/process large amounts of data.”
Data that is hard to get value from due to size and complexity.





Matter, Ulrich. 2024. Big Data Analytics: A Guide to Data Science Practitioners Making the Transition to Big Data. First edition. Chapman & Hall/CRC Data Science Series. CRC Press, Taylor & Francis Group. https://umatter.github.io/BigData/.

Loading data
The data is provided by you in a folder data/raw/. It is a good practice to separate raw data (e.g. extracted from a package, survey…) from final data derived from code calculations. Final data can always be regenerated programmatically, whereas raw data can’t.








Load the two datasets and assign them, respectively, to the variables proposals and votes.






















CautionQuestions about the data




How was the data sampled?





Initial exploration
It is good practice to do some initial exploration to familiarise with our data. Some questions we may want to immediately answer are:

How big are these datasets?
What do they contain?
How complete each variable are? (i.e., missing data)

We can explore the first rows using head(), or, conversely, use tail() to see the last rows.














CautionQUESTION: Why would we need to use one or the other (or both)?














Use the tail() and pass the dataframe as first parameter and the number of rows in the second one.


tail(proposals, 5)
tail(proposals, 5)









Alternative, dplyr provides an interesting function gplimpse to describe the dataframes:








However, for large datasets like these, it would probably be better to see explore them interactively within RStudio or Positron’s GUI by running:
View(proposals)






WarningDid you notice something wrong with the data?





The column draft_started contains dates, but the column type is a character. This can be an issue if we want to make computations (like we are going to do in the next section), so we will need to fix this.
This is not the only problematic column. Can you find any other changes?





Fixing data
To fix the problem we detected, we need to change draft_started column type to a date, and we will be using mutate() to do so.















NoteHint 1





We are looking for a column name here. We need to write the name of the column that we want to convert to a date.











TipFully worked solution:





proposals <- mutate(proposals, draft_started = as.Date(draft_started))













Tip



Note that this syntax would be equivalent to base R’s syntax:
proposals$draft_started <- as.Date(proposals$draft_started)
At this moment tidyverse syntax may seem a little bit confusing and not very useful, but maybe the next bits can change our minds.










But actually, it’s more common to write this code using the pipe operator1 |>:
1 This operator allows for chaining multiple operations together, streamlining code.
The pipe operator (|>) takes the value of its left-hand side to the first argument of the function on its right-hand side. This enables a natural and readable way of chaining multiple functions together, reducing the need for intermediate variables and improving code clarity.

# Nested, reads inside-out
round(mean(log(c(10, 100, 1000))), 2)

[1] 4.61

# Piped, reads left to right
c(10, 100, 1000) |> log() |> mean() |> round(2)

[1] 4.61
















Important



Bear with me: we will see why this syntax using the pipe operator |> is very convenient.

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
Answering questions through data

How diverse are the proposals?
On week 5 (Uprichard 2026), we saw the importance of measurments and how deciding what and how to measure is anything but trivial. There are many ways to define diversity. In this case, we will use the language in which the proposals are written as a proxy for diversity.

Uprichard, Emma. 2026. Lecture Slides - Week 5: Measurements. https://moodle.warwick.ac.uk/mod/resource/view.php?id=3277146.
We are going to use dplyr’s count() to count the number of different languages used in the column language.











proposals_lang <- proposals |> 
  count(language) # write the name of the columns

proposals_lang
proposals_lang <- proposals |> 
  count(language) # write the name of the columns

proposals_lang






count() conveniently can sort the values by number of uses:














CautionQuestion:



What does that information tell us? How is it related to diversity?




How much labour is required to make a proposal?
Again, there are multiple ways to define labour. One way could be to count time spent since their initial draft until the end of the voting process.






Important



Only a subset of proposals ever get to get voted, so we are going to use filter() to subset those proposals whose status is either Approved or Rejected and only select() the columns that are needed.


Here, we will be using select() to subset columns:











# Let's subset only the columns that are needed
time_spent_completed <- proposals |> 
  select(title, status_raw, draft_started, vote_end)

glimpse(time_spent_completed)

# Let's subset only the columns that are needed
time_spent_completed <- proposals |> 
  select(title, status_raw, draft_started, vote_end)

glimpse(time_spent_completed)


And now, let’s use filter() to subset rows whose status is either “Approved” or “Rejected”:










# Let's subset only the rows that are needed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  filter(status_raw %in% c("Approved", "Rejected"))

glimpse(time_spent_completed)
# Let's subset only the rows that are needed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  filter(status_raw %in% c("Approved", "Rejected"))

glimpse(time_spent_completed)










And now, we are going to compute the amount of time spent. We will be using mutate() to create a new variable called time_spent which is the time difference between the proposal was voted (finished) and drafted (started).










time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  mutate(time_spent = vote_end - draft_started)
  
time_spent_completed
time_spent_completed <- time_spent_completed |> 
  mutate(time_spent = vote_end - draft_started)
  
time_spent_completed








Tip



Remember when we spoke about the pipe operator |> ? We could pipe those two verbs in a single expression!










This new column time_spent says how much time each proposal took, in days2. We would need to have some nice summary statistics to have a good overview of the process.
2 Can you edit the code in the cell above to check time_spent data type? Is this what you would have expected?













Warning



We have some results that are either missing (NA) or negative values. This is because either the draft_started or vote_end values are missing. We should get rid of them to before proceeding.


But what if we wanted to see if there are differences between approved and rejected proposals? We will use group_by() to group by a variable and summarise(). to create new summary columns using some statistical functions:














CautionYour turn



Can you think of another variable we could use for measuring the labour involved? Could you do a similar process with this new variable?




How many votes did each proposal receive?
Votes are stored in a separate dataset proposals_votes, so let’s do some initial exploration














ImportantWide vs long data3



proposals_votes is a long dataset (as opposed to a wide one, like the previous one):

wide datasets: each row is an observation, refers to a unique value
long dataset: multiple rows refer to a same observation



3 For a more detailed explanation refer to https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/tidy-data.htmlWe could use what we’ve learnt to count the votes for each proposal and type of vote being cast:








We can remove the proposals with no votes:









Reshaping dataframes
This format is not very useful for us now. It would be better to see how many votes of each type a proposal has received. In other words, we need to convert from a long format to a wide format. To do so, we will use another package from the tidyverse: {tidyr} provides two convenient functions pivot_wider()4 to convert from long to wide, and pivot_longer(), to do the opposite.
4 This function is full of nuances and requires having a clear picture of the actual data and what the shape we want it to have. Refer to the vignette vignette::pivot_wider or the help function ?pivot_wider









Combining dataframes
We have two datasets: one containing proposals, and another one containing votes. Wouldn’t it be nice to have the total votes per proposal in a single dataset?
To combine proposals with proposals_votes, we need to:

Make sure that both dataframes have a shared field to use as an index
Make sure that both dataframes are either long or wide

Gladly, both conditions are met, so we are ready to join them.










Piping everything
Or, we could do all of this (and something more) piping multiple verbs in one statement:

Can you guess what additional steps did we do and what are their outcomes?

title: 1. Interrogating data locally
text:
Further questions
By now, you should be equipped to answer the following questions by adapting the code above:

What gets proposed?
What’s the general outcome of the tagging proposal?
What are the more controversial proposals?

And questions related to measurement:

Has this process or its outcomes changed over time?
How can we operationalise diversity?
